rows.speaker: الأصمعي
rows.claim: Al-Aṣmaʿī reads سلكى as a straight stab and مخلوجة as one veering right or left, like two arrows that do not land alike.
rows.anchor: وفسره الأصمعي فقال: أراد نطعنهم طعنة سلكى، أي مستوية

rows.speaker: زيد بن كثوة العنبري
rows.claim: Zayd says people misquote the line: it is كر كلامين على نابل, two stabs delivered without pause, like telling an archer twice to shoot; he prefers this sense.
rows.anchor: وقال الزيادي : كان زيد بن كثوة العنبري يقول: الناس يغلطون في لفظ هذا البيت ومعناه

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: One view makes العير a tent peg, named for its protrusion like the raised middle of an arrowhead; the line blames the group for every tent-dweller’s offense.
rows.anchor: فكان بعضهم يجعله الوتد، سماه عيرا لنتوئه مثل عير نصل السهم

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Another view identifies العير with Kulaib Waʾil, the chief, deriving the title from the onager as the largest wild animal.
rows.anchor: وقال بعضهم: هو كليب وائل، والعير: سيد القوم، سمي بذلك لأن العير أكبر الوحش

rows.speaker: رسول الله
rows.claim: The Prophet told Abu Sufyan, «كل الصيد في جوف العير», a report used to support العير as the greatest beast.
rows.anchor: قال رسول الله، صلى الله عليه وسلم، لأبي سفيان

rows.speaker: آخر
rows.claim: A further view makes العير a mountain near Medina and invokes the Prophet’s prohibition of the area between ʿAyr and Thawr; the line implicates anyone reaching that place.
rows.anchor: وقال آخر: العير جبل بالمدينة، ومنه: أن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم حرم ما بين عير إلى ثور

rows.speaker: آخر
rows.claim: Another interpretation takes العير literally as a donkey: the group is blamed for the offenses of everyone who drives one.
rows.anchor: وقال آخر: هو الحمار نفسه، يريد أنفسهم يضيفون إلينا ذنوب كل من ساق حمارا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Qutayba sums up the views: the speakers are saddled with everyone’s sins and treated as their allies.
rows.anchor: ومعنى هذا كله: أنهم يلزموننا بذنوب الناس جميعا، ويجعلوننا أولياءهم

rows.speaker: الأصمعي
rows.claim: Al-Aṣmaʿī cannot determine two phrases by Ruʾba: the line about الأهيغ seems to imply water, and he also does not know كأنه حامل جنب أخذعا.
rows.anchor: وقال الأصمعي: لا أدري ما معنى قول رؤبة

rows.speaker: ابن الأعرابي
rows.claim: Ibn al-Aʿrābī says منغمس في الأهيغين means absorbed in eating and sex; the two الأطيبان likewise mean food and sex.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن الأعرابي : يقال: فلان منغمس في الأهيغين، يراد: الأكل والنكاح

rows.speaker: ابن الأعرابي
rows.claim: Ibn al-Aʿrābī explains that a sword blow left the bull’s side hanging as it leaned; خذع means inclination.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن الأعرابي: أراد: كأنه ضرب بالسيف ضربة

words: مَآ أَغْنَىٰ عَنْهُ مَالُهُۥ وَمَا كَسَبَ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He objects to the prior point as difficult to reconcile with God describing the person as having wealth and offspring, citing the verse about his wealth and earnings.
rows.anchor: ولست أدري كيف هذا لأن الله عز وجل وصفه بالمال والولد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although many restrict مسد to palm fiber, Ibn Qutayba says it means anything braided and twisted, from fiber or another material.
rows.anchor: إنما المسد: كل ما ضفر وفتل من الليف وغيره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: مسد means a twisted thing, as in twisting rope; fallen fruit and leaves are similarly named after نفض and خبط.
rows.anchor: يقال: مسدت الحبل مسدا إذا فتلته، فهو مسد

rows.speaker: الراجز
rows.claim: An anonymous rajaz poet addresses a palm-leaf cord as مسد, showing the word can refer to plant fiber.
rows.anchor: قول الراجز : يا مسد الخوص تعوذ مني

rows.speaker: آخر
rows.claim: Another poet calls a cord made from camel hides مسد, showing that the word is not limited to plant fiber.
rows.anchor: وقال آخر : ومسد أمر من أيانق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ممسود الخلق describes a body that is sinewy, twisted, and corded.
rows.anchor: ومنه قيل: رجل ممسود الخلق، إذا كان مجدولا مفتولا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās identifies the مسد as the chain mentioned in the verse describing a chain seventy cubits long.
rows.anchor: فاسلكوه [الحاقة: 32] . كذلك قال ابن عباس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The chain may be called مسد even if made of iron or fire, since the name can refer to braiding and twisting.
rows.anchor: فيجوز أن يكون سماها مسدا، وإن كانت حديدا أو نارا

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda takes اللهو in the verse about taking amusement as a woman.
rows.anchor: قال قتادة والحسن: اللهو: المرأة

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan also interprets اللهو as a woman.
rows.anchor: قال قتادة والحسن: اللهو: المرأة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās interprets اللهو as a child.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس: هو الولد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The woman and child interpretations are close: a man’s wife and child are called his two fragrant joys.
rows.anchor: والتفسيران متقاربان، لأن امرأة الرجل لهوه، وولده لهوه ولذلك يقال: امرأة الرجل وولده ريحانتاه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: اللهو originally means intercourse, euphemistically replacing it like السر; the woman is then called لهو because intercourse occurs with her.
rows.anchor: وأصل اللهو: الجماع، فكني عنه باللهو، كما كني عنه بالسر

rows.speaker: امرؤ القيس
rows.claim: Imruʾ al-Qays uses اللهو to mean intercourse; a variant of his line has السر with the same meaning.
rows.anchor: امرؤ القيس : ألا زعمت بسباسة اليوم أنني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In context, God answers Christians’ claims about Jesus and his mother: if He wanted a consort and child as they claim, He would take them from Himself, not from them.
rows.anchor: وتأويل الآية: أن النصارى لما قالت في المسيح وأمه ما قالت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: أو can express doubt, as in saying that one saw ʿAbd Allāh or Muḥammad.
rows.anchor: أو: تأتي للشك، تقول. رأيت عبد الله أو محمدا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: أو can offer a choice between alternatives; any one of the stated expiations or sacrifices suffices.
rows.anchor: وتكون للتخيير بين شيئين، كقوله: فكفارته إطعام عشرة مساكين

rows.speaker: المفسرون
rows.claim: Exegetes take أو as واو in examples such as عذرا أو نذرا, لعله يتذكر أو يخشى, and لعلهم يتقون أو يحدث لهم ذكرا.
rows.anchor: هذا كله عند المفسرين بمعنى واو النسق

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some interpreters read أو as بل in these verses, correcting or retracting the preceding statement.
rows.anchor: فإن بعضهم يذهب إلى أنها بمعنى بل يزيدون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Qutayba rejects بل and prefers واو in all three examples: the audience exceeds one hundred thousand, the Hour is nearer, and the distance was a bow’s length and more.
rows.anchor: وإنما هي بمعنى (الواو) في جميع هذه المواضع

rows.speaker: ابن أحمر
rows.claim: Ibn Aḥmar uses أو for واو: he was kept away for two months and half of a third, not two months or half a third month.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن أحمر : قرى عنكما شهرين أو نصف ثالث

rows.speaker: آخر
rows.claim: An anonymous poet uses أو coordinatively in a paired comparison, meaning he balanced these two groups against those two.
rows.anchor: وقال آخر : أثعلبة الفوارس أو رياحا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Qutayba groups examples where number or pronouns do not repeat each coordinated item, including singular predicates for paired terms.
rows.anchor: وقال: عن اليمين وعن الشمال قعيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In عن اليمين وعن الشمال قعيد, قعيد is understood twice: one watcher sits on the right and another on the left.
rows.anchor: أراد: عن اليمين قعيد وعن الشمال قعيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arabic and Qurʾanic speech may address listeners in the second person and then refer to them in the third person.
rows.anchor: ومنه أن تخاطب الشاهد بشيء ثم تجعل الخطاب له على لفظ الغائب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage begins with كنتم, then shifts to بهم and فرحوا while describing the same people.
rows.anchor: حتى إذا كنتم في الفلك وجرين بهم بريح طيبة وفرحوا بها

rows.speaker: الشاعر
rows.claim: The poet addresses Mayya’s home, then describes it in the third person as fallen silent.
rows.anchor: قال الشاعر : يا دار مية بالعلياء فالسند

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reverse shift also occurs: speech can directly address someone after referring to that person as absent.
rows.anchor: وكذلك أيضا تجعل خطاب الغائب للشاهد

rows.speaker: الهذلي
rows.claim: The Hudhalī poem illustrates a shift from third-person reference to direct second-person address.
rows.anchor: كقول الهذلي : يا ويح نفسي كان جدة خالد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A passage may first address the Prophet, then turn to the unbelievers; the following command and question clarify the new addressees.
rows.anchor: الخطاب للنبي، صلى الله عليه وسلم، ثم قال للكفار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Qutayba cites shifts in addressee, including a question to Moses and Aaron that names Moses alone, and a reference to humanity’s father Adam.
rows.anchor: وقال: فمن ربكما يا موسى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The dual pronoun addresses Moses and Aaron even though the vocative names Moses alone.
rows.anchor: وقال: فمن ربكما يا موسى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arabic can use a dual-form command when addressing one, two, or more people; the segment ends before Ibn Qutayba gives examples.
rows.anchor: ومنه أن تأمر الواحد والاثنين والثلاثة فما فوق أمرك الاثنين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The root meaning of هدى is to guide; in the cited prayers it means أرشدنا, guide us.
rows.anchor: أصل هدى أرشد، كقوله: عسى ربي أن يهديني سواء السبيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In examples about Thamūd and former peoples inheriting the earth, هدى means to make clear or show: guidance by explanation.
rows.anchor: فالإرشاد في جميع هذه بالبيان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: هدى can mean to summon: a hādī is a prophet who calls his people, and the cited leaders and Prophet call people.
rows.anchor: ومنها إرشاد بالدعاء، كقوله: ولكل قوم هاد

words: أَعْطَىٰ كُلَّ شَىْءٍ خَلْقَهُۥ ثُمَّ هَدَىٰ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God gives each creature its form, including male or female form, then inspires it to approach the female, seek pasture, and avoid dangers.
rows.anchor: الذي أعطى كل شيء خلقه ثم هدى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the other verse, God guides the male by inspiration to approach the female.
rows.anchor: والذي قدر فهدى (3) [الأعلى: 3] ، أي هدى الذكر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: هدى can mean carry out or bring to completion; God does not execute or make the treacherous plot succeed.
rows.anchor: ومنها إرشاد بالإمضاء، كقوله: وأن الله لا يهدي كيد الخائنين

rows.speaker: آخر
rows.claim: An alternative gloss says that God does not repair or set right the treacherous plot.
rows.anchor: ويقال: لا يصلحه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The various senses of guidance are related to one another.
rows.anchor: وبعض هذا قريب من بعض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In ولأصلبنكم في جذوع النخل, في is used for على: they will crucify people on the palm trunks.
rows.anchor: قوله تعالى: ولأصلبنكم في جذوع النخل

rows.speaker: الشاعر
rows.claim: The poet’s line about crucifying al-ʿAbdī في جذع نخلة uses في to mean on a palm trunk.
rows.anchor: قال الشاعر : وهم صلبوا العبدي في جذع نخلة

rows.speaker: عنترة
rows.claim: ʿAntara says a hero’s clothes are في a tree, meaning on it because of his height.
rows.anchor: وقال عنترة : بطل كأن ثيابه في سرحة

rows.speaker: دريد بن الصمة
rows.claim: In Duraid’s line, ظنوا means be sure of the enemy’s arrival, not merely suspect it.
rows.anchor: قال دريد بن الصمة : فقلت لهم: ظنوا بألفي مدجح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: عسى and لعل can express certainty as well as doubt; لعلهم يهتدون here means so that they may be guided.
rows.anchor: وكذلك جعلوا (عسى) شكا ويقينا، (ولعل) شكا ويقينا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: شار can name buyer or seller because each buys in the exchange; شرى in the cited verses means sold.
rows.anchor: وللمشتري: شار، وللبائع: شار، لأن كل واحد منهما اشترى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The seller can also be called بائع because he sells and takes compensation for what he gives.
rows.anchor: وكذلك قولهم لكل واحد منهما: (بائع) لأنه باع وأخذ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qurʾanic verb شرى can mean sold: they sold the boy for a low price and sold their own souls for an evil bargain.
rows.anchor: قال الله عز وجل: وشروه بثمن بخس دراهم

rows.speaker: ابن مفرغ
rows.claim: Ibn Mufarrigh uses شريت to mean I sold; Bard was a slave the poet sold and regretted selling.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن مفرغ : وشريت بردا ليتني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: وراء means behind or in front: whatever is hidden from sight lies beyond one’s view; in two cited verses it means ahead of them.
rows.anchor: و (وراء) تكون بمعنى (خلف) وبمعنى (قدام)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: جلل can describe either great or small: each is large beside something smaller and small beside something larger.
rows.anchor: وقالوا للكبير: (جلل) ، وللصغير: (جلل)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: بعض can mean كل because an entire thing is also a part relative to something larger.
rows.anchor: ولهذا جعلت (بعض) بمعنى (كل) ، لأن الشيء يكون كله بعضا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Conversely, كل can mean بعض, as in the Queen’s having everything, provisions from everywhere, or the wind destroying everything.
rows.anchor: (وكل) بمعنى (بعض) ، كقوله: وأوتيت من كل شيء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: فوق may mean دون and دون may mean فوق when comparison is relative to what is above or below.
rows.anchor: وجعلت (فوق) بمعنى (دون) في قول الله عز وجل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: خشينا can mean علمنا: the speaker knew the boy would overwhelm his parents with rebellion and disbelief.
rows.anchor: و (خشيت) بمعنى: (علمت)

rows.speaker: أبي
rows.claim: The reading attributed to Ubayy has فخاف ربك in place of the canonical wording.
rows.anchor: وفي قراءة أبي: فخاف ربك

rows.speaker: الحطيئة
rows.claim: Al-Ḥuṭayʾa reverses the syntax: the hoof holds the rope, rather than the rope holding the hoof; each holds the other while attached.
rows.anchor: قال الحطيئة : فلما خشيت الهون والعير ممسك

rows.speaker: الأخطل
rows.claim: Al-Akhṭal reverses the roles; the intended sense is that the group’s backsides reached Najrān and Hajar, since what one reaches also reaches one.
rows.anchor: وقال الأخطل : على العيارات هداجون قد بلغت

rows.speaker: آخر
rows.claim: An anonymous poet puts الأفعوان and الشجاع in the accusative where the expected construction makes them nominative, since allies act on one another.
rows.anchor: وقال آخر : قد سالم الحيات منه القدما

rows.speaker: الشماخ
rows.claim: Al-Shammākh reverses agent and object in عصب العلباء بالعود; the expected order is عصب العود بالعلباء, though either construction is used.
rows.anchor: وقال الشماخ يذكر أباه : منه ولدت ولم يؤشب به حسبي

rows.speaker: ذو الرمة
rows.claim: Dhū al-Rummah reverses object and recipient: he means clothing the waist with a shield, since كسوت can take the garment or its wearer as object.
rows.anchor: وقال ذو الرمة : وتكسو المجن الرخو خصرا

rows.speaker: أبو النجم
rows.claim: Abū al-Najm reverses what approaches what: he means the constellation approaching the horizon, since each draws near to the other.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو النجم : قبل دنو الأفق من جوزائه

rows.speaker: الراعي
rows.claim: Al-Rāʿī says hunters see the eye as a track, where the expected phrasing is that they see the track as clearly as an eye; the inversion is reciprocal.
rows.anchor: وقال الراعي يصف ثورا : فصبحته كلاب الغوث يوسدها

rows.speaker: النابغة
rows.claim: Al-Nābigha reverses the comparison of fears; he means the antelope’s fear is no greater than his own, so their fears are equal.
rows.anchor: وقال النابغة : وقد خفت حتى ما تزيد مخافتي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: حزن describes elevated, rough ground; if it rises a little more, it is حزم.
rows.anchor: ولما ارتفع من الأرض: حزن فإن زاد قليلا قيل: حزم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A person who feels cold is خصر; if also hungry, the word is خرص.
rows.anchor: وللذي يجد البرد: خصر فإن كان مع ذلك جوع قيل: خرص

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A fire that has gone out is هامدة; خامدة describes one whose flame died while embers remain.
rows.anchor: وللنار إذا طفئت: هامدة فإن سكن اللهب وبقي من جمرها شيء قيل: خامدة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The source distinguishes صائم, a person made stationary by injury, from صائن, one whose standing results from foot injury or soreness.
rows.anchor: وللقائم من الخبل: صائم فإن كان ذلك من حفى أو وجى، قيل: صائن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: شكد is a gift; شكم is one given in requital.
rows.anchor: وللعطاء: شكد فإن كان مكافأة قيل: شكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: غلط is an unintentional mistake generally, while غلت is an error in calculation.
rows.anchor: وللخطأ من غير التعمد: غلط فإن كان في الحساب قيل: غلت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: خوص describes a narrow eye; حوص refers to narrowness at its rear corner.
rows.anchor: وللضيق في العين: خوص فإن كان ذلك في مؤخرها قيل: حوص

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arabic derives terms for belly conditions: مبطن for lean, بطين for naturally large, مبطان from overeating, بطن for a glutton, and مبطون for a belly ailment.
rows.anchor: كاشتقاقهم من البطن للخميص: مبطن وللعظيم البطن إذا كان خلقة: بطين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: وجد can mean finding a lost object, anger, sadness, or self-sufficiency; its nouns vary respectively as وجود or وجدانا, وجدا, موجدة, and وجدا.
rows.anchor: ثم يجعلون الاسم الضالة: وجودا ووجدانا وفي الحزن وجدا وفي الغضب موجدة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arabic poetry serves as a book: a storehouse of knowledge, guardian of etiquette, record of genealogies, and durable register of history.
rows.anchor: وللعرب الشعر الذي أقامه الله تعالى لها مقام الكتاب لغيرها، وجعله لعلومها مستودعا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Meter, rhyme, ordering, and careful choice protect poetry from falsification, which is easier in prose.
rows.anchor: وحرسه بالوزن، والقوافي، وحسن النظم، وجودة التخيير- من التدليس والتغيير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Departures from poetic convention are called sinād, iqwāʾ, ikfāʾ, or iṭwāʾ; this segment defines sinād and begins iqwāʾ.
rows.anchor: وقد تجد الشاعر منهم ربما زال عن سننهم شيئا، فيقولون له: ساندت، وأقويت، وأكفأت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sinād involves differing rhyme supports or letters before them; ʿAmr ibn Kulthūm’s lines contrast kasra in فأصبحينا with fatḥa in جرينا.
rows.anchor: كقول عمرو بن كلثوم : ألا هبي بصحنك فاصبحينا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Iqwāʾ is described as a letter omitted from the first hemistich; the promised poetic example is not included here.
rows.anchor: وخالف في (الإقواء) بحرف نقصه من شطر البيت الأول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Qutayba rejects the claim that only God knows the Qurʾan’s ambiguous passages, calling it a mistake of language and interpretation.
rows.anchor: ولسنا ممن يزعم: أن المتشابه في القرآن لا يعلمه الراسخون في العلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God sent every part of the Qurʾan to benefit people and point to its intended meaning; otherwise critics could attack it over passages no one can understand.
rows.anchor: ولم ينزل الله شيئا من القرآن إلا لينفع به عباده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the Prophet knew the interpretation, learned Companions could know it too; Ibn Qutayba says God taught ʿAlī exegesis.
rows.anchor: وهل يجوز لأحد أن يقول

rows.speaker: رسول الله
rows.claim: The Prophet prayed that Ibn ʿAbbās be taught interpretation and given understanding of religion.
rows.anchor: ودعا لابن عباس فقال: «اللهم علمه التأويل، وفقهه في الدين»

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās once said he knew all the Qurʾan except four terms—ghislīn, ḥanān, al-awwāh, al-raqīm—but Ibn Qutayba says he later learned them.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس أنه قال: كل القرآن أعلم إلا أربعا

words: وَٱلرَّٰسِخُونَ فِى ٱلْعِلْمِ يَقُولُونَ ءَامَنَّا بِهِۦ
rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid glosses the learned as learning the interpretation and then saying, “We believe in it.”
rows.anchor: عن مجاهد قال: تعلمونه وتقولون: آمنا به

words: وَٱلرَّٰسِخُونَ فِى ٱلْعِلْمِ يَقُولُونَ ءَامَنَّا بِهِۦ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If scholars only say they believe all comes from God, they have no distinction over ordinary learners or ignorant Muslims; they must have interpretive knowledge.
rows.anchor: لم يكن للراسخين فضل على المتعلمين، بل على جهلة المسلمين

rows.speaker: المفسرون
rows.claim: Ibn Qutayba says exegetes interpreted every part of the Qurʾan rather than declaring anything unknowable, including the disconnected letters at sūra openings.
rows.anchor: فإنا لم نر المفسرين توقفوا عن شيء من القرآن

words: وَمَا يَعْلَمُ تَأْوِيلَهُۥٓ إِلَّا ٱللَّهُ وَٱلرَّٰسِخُونَ
rows.speaker: كثير من النحويين
rows.claim: Many grammarians argue that coordinating the learned with God leaves يقولون without a conjunction assigning them a second action; Ibn Qutayba presents this as an objection behind some interpreters’ error.
rows.anchor: وهذا مذهب كثير من النحويين في هذه الآية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Qutayba places Abraham in an age of astrology and divination, when people revered stars and claimed they foretold hidden events; Nimrod ordered newborns killed after astrologers predicted Abraham’s birth.
rows.anchor: عصر نجوم وكهانة، وإنما أمر نمروذ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham looked into astrological calculation, not at the stars: the wording has في rather than إلى, as when one studies astrology, law, arithmetic, or grammar.
rows.anchor: فنظر نظرة في النجوم، يريد علم النجوم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham pretended to share the people’s astrological knowledge to deceive them and avoid their outing; إني سقيم means he would inevitably become sick and could not go.
rows.anchor: وإنما أراد بالنظر فيها: أن يوهمهم أنه يعلم منها ما يعلمون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: إنك ميت addressed to the Prophet means he will die, not that he was already dead; Ibn Qutayba compares this future certainty to Abraham’s wording.
rows.anchor: ومثله قوله تعالى: إنك ميت وإنهم ميتون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: لعمرك and ولعمر الله mean “by your life” and “by God’s life”; they are oaths sworn by life.
rows.anchor: لعمرك، ولعمر الله: هو العمر. ويقال: أطال الله عمرك، وعمرك، وهو قسم بالبقاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The conditional means “if, according to your claim, the Merciful has a child”; the Prophet should answer that he would be first to worship God as a monotheist.
rows.anchor: قل إن كان للرحمن ولد فأنا أول العابدين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Whoever affirms God’s unity worships Him; whoever assigns Him a child or partner is not a worshipper, however devout.
rows.anchor: ومن وحد الله فقد عبده، ومن جعل له ولدا أو ندا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the verse on creating jinn and humans, يعبدون means يوحدون, to affirm divine unity.
rows.anchor: وما خلقت الجن والإنس إلا ليعبدون

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid says that if God had a child as opponents claim, the Prophet would be first to worship and affirm unity, denying their claim.
rows.anchor: قال مجاهد : يريد إن كان لله ولد في قولكم

rows.speaker: بعض المفسرين
rows.claim: Some exegetes take إن as negation meaning ما; Ibn Qutayba says he does not favor this.
rows.anchor: وبعض المفسرين يجعل إن بمعنى (ما)

rows.speaker: آخر
rows.claim: Another gloss takes العابدون as the angry or indignant, from عبد من كذا, “to be angered by something.”
rows.anchor: ويقال: العابدون هاهنا: الغضاب الآنفون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Active nouns from فَعِلَ يَفْعَلُ usually follow فَعِل, sometimes فاعل; عبد يعبد allows both عبد and عابد.
rows.anchor: وأكثر ما تأتي الأسماء من فعل يفعل (على فعل)

rows.speaker: امرؤ القيس
rows.claim: Imruʾ al-Qays’s line وأعبد أن تهجى تميم بدارم attests indignation at an insult to Tamīm.
rows.anchor: قال الشاعر : وأعبد أن تهجى تميم بدارم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: مثل الجنة means its likeness, description, and qualities.
rows.anchor: فأراد الله بقوله: مثل الجنة، أي صورتها وصفتها

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: A report says ʿAlī read مثال الجنة or أمثال الجنة; either equals مثل but is clearer as description.
rows.anchor: وروي أن عليا رحمه الله كان يقرأ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In 48:29, مثلهم means their description, since the passage describes believers rather than first presenting a comparison.
rows.anchor: لأنه لم يضرب لهم مثلا في أول الكلام، فيقول: ذلك مثلهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fly passage implies rather than states the comparison: idol worshippers resemble people unable to create a fly or recover what it steals.
rows.anchor: ولم يأت بالمثل، لأن في الكلام معناه، كأنه قال: يا أيها الناس

words: إِنَّ ٱلَّذِينَ تَدْعُونَ مِن دُونِ ٱللَّهِ لَن يَخْلُقُوا۟ ذُبَابًا
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Qutayba says comparable implicit parables occur elsewhere in the Qurʾan and Arabic, treated in his chapters on figurative language.
rows.anchor: ومثل هذا في القرآن وكلام العرب أشياء قد اقتصصناها

words: وَإِن مَّا نُرِيَنَّكَ بَعْضَ ٱلَّذِى نَعِدُهُمْ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Whether the Prophet sees part of the promised punishment in life or dies before seeing it, his duty is only to convey; God handles the reckoning.
rows.anchor: وإن ما نرينك بعض الذي نعدهم أو نتوفينك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The governor analogy divides roles: an envoy warns and reports resistance, while the ruler decides punishment and recompense; the envoy should not demand action.
rows.anchor: إنما عليك التبليغ والعظة، وعلينا الجزاء والمكافأة
